Thus, although the 1953 Order may be relevant, it is not determinative of the matter.
holdings.statement: The 1953 Order is relevant but not determinative of whether different language can transfer less than an absolute interest in land.

holdings.quote: Moreover, relying on indirect evidence, such as the language of an earlier Order in Council, would require me not only to interpret the Seabird Order, but first to interpret the earlier Order to establish a framework for comparison. Only then might it be possible to glean some help from the language in one Order, in deciding the intention of the other. Given the factual record in this appeal, this Court cannot engage in that inquiry.
holdings.statement: The Court cannot engage in interpreting an earlier Order to help interpret the Seabird Order given the factual record, so indirect evidence from earlier Orders is not helpful here.

holdings.quote: Consequently, I am not persuaded that there was a clear and plain intention to entirely extinguish the aboriginal interest in this land.
holdings.statement: There is no clear and plain intention to entirely extinguish the aboriginal interest in the land from the Seabird Order.

holdings.quote: Although the parties have not emphasized it, a word should be said about the 1961 agreement to give permission to the British Columbia Electric Company Limited to "construct ... and maintain upon the Reserve poles ... and one or more lines of wire for the distribution of electrical energy and for communication and television purposes." All parties to that agreement expressly realized that permission was necessary because the land was "Reserve land within the meaning of the Indian Act", as it read at the time. If the permission was sought and granted with respect to land in the corridor, then to me, it would be nearly incontrovertible that such land was admitted, by the parties to that agreement, to be subject to the Band's interest.
holdings.statement: The 1961 agreement granting permission to erect power lines on Reserve land shows the parties recognized the land was Reserve land under the Indian Act at the time.

holdings.quote: The question is, therefore, whether this agreement specifically contemplates land in the corridor or not. The agreement states that the Reserve is "situate, lying and being on Seabird Island". It does not, however, state that the Reserve is the whole of Seabird Island. Thus, it is unclear whether the agreement refers to the whole island or simply most of the island, excepting out the part containing the Lougheed Highway corridor. It might be possible to infer that if the parties to this agreement contemplated that it did not relate to the Lougheed Highway corridor, since that land was not "Reserve land", they might have said so. Alternatively, it is possible to infer from the omission of such a statement, that such a point was so obvious it did not require mentioning. To me, either inference is legitimate. A reference to particular land is found in the Band Council Resolution, which expressly states that the agreement sought specifically to accommodate an extension to a power line "along the Seabird Island roadway adjacent to the Maria Slough as shown on Pole Plan No. 24239 dated June 15, 1961." That Plan is not in evidence, and there is no indication whether the roadway referred to is in or near the corridor. As it is unclear whether this agreement, in fact, evinces a concession that the Lougheed Highway corridor was "Reserve land" and, therefore, subject to the Band's interest, it is a neutral factor with respect to the interpretation of the Seabird Order. 4.
holdings.statement: It is unclear whether the 1961 agreement specifically contemplates land in the Lougheed Highway corridor or not, so it is a neutral factor in interpreting the Seabird Order.

holdings.quote: In sum, although the language of the Order and the context surrounding this case are virtually identical to the facts in Osoyoos, supra, there are several differences here. To review, first, the express language of the reservation of mines and minerals is slightly different. Second, the language of the provincial legislation is different. Third, whereas the canal was already constructed, the highway was not. Fourth, the language of an earlier Order in Council refers specifically to the "use" of land. Finally, a 1961 agreement acknowledges that the permission of the federal government was necessary to erect power lines on Reserve land. The crucial question, therefore, is whether the slight differences in the terms of the transfer, in conjunction with additional contextual evidence not present in Osoyoos, establish a clear and plain intention to extinguish completely the aboriginal interest in the corridor.
holdings.statement: Several differences from Osoyoos exist, including differences in reservation language, provincial legislation, construction status, earlier Orders, and the 1961 agreement, which must be considered to determine if there was a clear and plain intention to extinguish aboriginal interest.

holdings.quote: I cannot say they do. Nothing in this case is sufficient to differentiate it from Osoyoos, supra, so as to establish a "clear and plain" intention to completely extinguish the aboriginal interest in the corridor.
holdings.statement: The differences do not establish a clear and plain intention to extinguish the aboriginal interest in the corridor.

holdings.quote: The language of the Seabird Order, like the Osoyoos Order, is genuinely ambiguous. In conclusion, as explained in Osoyoos, supra at para. 68, "the interpretation that impairs the Indian interests as little as possible should be preferred, so long as the ambiguity is a genuine one".
holdings.statement: The language of the Seabird Order is genuinely ambiguous and must be interpreted in a way that impairs Indian interests as little as possible.

holdings.quote: The provincial legislation cannot be determinative of anything, but only acts as a constraint placed upon the Crown to grant only an interest that is within the scope of the province's own statutory power.
holdings.statement: Provincial legislation only constrains the Crown's grant to what is within provincial statutory power and is not determinative of extinguishment.

holdings.quote: Moreover, I am not persuaded that the construction and maintenance of the corridor necessarily required an absolute extinguishment of the aboriginal interest. In fact, the circumstances suggest the opposite.
holdings.statement: Construction and maintenance of the corridor did not necessarily require absolute extinguishment of aboriginal interest; circumstances suggest otherwise.

holdings.quote: The language of the 1953 Order is merely one of the ways, but certainly not the only way, that the federal government might have transferred less than an absolute interest in land. The 1961 agreement does little or nothing to supplement the analysis.
holdings.statement: The 1953 Order is one way but not the only way the federal government might transfer less than an absolute interest in land; the 1961 agreement does little to supplement this analysis.

holdings.quote: Embracing that principle, I have concluded, as I am bound to do, that because of the genuine ambiguity in the Seabird Order, it must be interpreted to mean that the entire aboriginal interest in the Lougheed Highway corridor was not extinguished.
holdings.statement: Because of the genuine ambiguity, the Seabird Order must be interpreted to mean the entire aboriginal interest in the Lougheed Highway corridor was not extinguished.

holdings.quote: To borrow the words of Iacobucci J., therefore, I cannot say that "the entire interest of a band is removed" and, consequently, "land remains in the reserve for the purposes of s. 83(1)(a)" (Osoyoos, supra at para. 50). Given that the Band retains its interest in land "in the reserve", it is unnecessary for me to identify precisely the interest granted to the province. Suffice it to say that the Order in Council falls short of completely extinguishing the "entire interest" of the Band and, therefore, the Band is entitled to exercise the powers granted by s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act.
holdings.statement: The Band retains its interest in land 'in the reserve' and thus is entitled to exercise powers under s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act; the Order in Council does not completely extinguish the Band's entire interest.

holdings.quote: Thus, the Appeal Judge's decision cannot stand in light of Osoyoos, supra.
holdings.statement: The Appeal Judge's decision cannot stand in light of Osoyoos.

holdings.quote: I should end by addressing the potential misapprehension that the result of the corridor being "in the reserve" for the purposes of s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act is to enable the Band to wreak havoc with the maintenance and operation of the road itself or any other interest in the corridor. In fact, this is not the case.
holdings.statement: The corridor being "in the reserve" under s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act does not allow the Band to disrupt the maintenance and operation of the road or other interests in the corridor.

holdings.quote: Also, even under the Indian Act, the Band does not have an unfettered right to enact by-laws that are incompatible with the interest created pursuant to s. 35 (Osoyoos, supra at para. 75).
holdings.statement: The Band does not have an unfettered right under the Indian Act to enact by-laws incompatible with interests created under s. 35.

holdings.quote: Indeed, the result for the respondent in particular is merely that it must pay its taxes to the Band rather than the District of Kent.
holdings.statement: The practical effect for the respondent is that it must pay taxes to the Band rather than the District of Kent.

holdings.quote: Because, for purpose of s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act, the Band's entire interest in the Lougheed Highway corridor was not removed from the Reserve, it is unnecessary for me to consider whether the land would revert back to the Band had the aboriginal interest been completely extinguished.
holdings.statement: Because the Band's entire interest in the Lougheed Highway corridor was not removed from the Reserve for the purpose of s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act, it is unnecessary to consider whether the land would revert back to the Band if the aboriginal interest had been completely extinguished.

holdings.quote: This appeal should be allowed, the decision of the Appeal Judge should be set aside and the appeal from the Seabird Island Indian Band Board Review should be dismissed with costs to the appellant of his appeal and in the Trial Division.
holdings.statement: The appeal is allowed, the decision of the Appeal Judge is set aside, and the appeal from the Seabird Island Indian Band Board Review is dismissed with costs to the appellant of his appeal and in the Trial Division.

holdings.quote: In my respectful view, the reasoning of the Supreme Court in Osoyoos Indian Band, supra, supports the conclusion reached by the Appeal Judge in this case.
holdings.statement: The reasoning of the Supreme Court in Osoyoos Indian Band supports the conclusion reached by the Appeal Judge in this case.

holdings.quote: I agree that the wording of the Order in Council with which we are concerned is strikingly similar to the one reviewed by the Supreme Court in Osoyoos.
holdings.statement: The wording of the Order in Council in this case is strikingly similar to the one reviewed by the Supreme Court in Osoyoos.

holdings.quote: However, there are two crucial differences which, in my respectful view, would have led the majority to reach a different result in Osoyoos.
holdings.statement: There are two crucial differences between the Orders in Council here and in Osoyoos that would have led the majority to reach a different result in Osoyoos.

holdings.quote: Section 35 clearly permits the taking of reserve land for public purposes. Moreover, it is clear and plain that s. 35 authorizes the taking or use of a range of interests in land, up to and including a fee simple interest. This is obvious from an ordinary and grammatical reading of the words of the section.
holdings.statement: Section 35 of the Indian Act permits the taking of reserve land for public purposes and authorizes the taking or use of a range of interests in land, up to and including a fee simple interest.

holdings.quote: In seeking to expropriate reserve land under s. 35(1) of the Indian Act, the Province was only able to take or use land that it was empowered to take under an Act of the provincial legislature. Section 35(1) reads: 35. (1) Where by an Act of ... a provincial legislature Her Majesty in right of a province ... is empowered to take or to use lands or any interest therein without the consent of the owner, the power may, with the consent of the Governor in Council ... be exercised in relation to lands in a reserve or any interest therein. [Emphasis in original] The words "the power" clearly refer to that power contained in the Act of the provincial legislature referred to in the opening lines of s. 35(1). Thus, the Province could only exercise "the power" given to it by the relevant Act of the legislature.
holdings.statement: Section 35(1) authorizes the Province to exercise only the power given to it by an Act of the provincial legislature to take or use lands in a reserve, with the consent of the Governor in Council.

holdings.quote: The parties concede that the Minister of Agriculture applied for the lands at issue under s. 21 of the Water Act, as inferred from the recitations of the Order in Council, i.e. "the Minister of Agriculture ... applied for the lands ... for irrigation canal purposes". Section 21 of the Water Act provides: 21.__(1) In this and the following three sections "land" includes any estate or interest in or easement over land. (2) Every licensee shall have the right to expropriate any land reasonably required for the construction, maintenance, improvement, or operation of any works authorized under his licence ... Thus, under s. 21 of the Water Act, the Minister of Agriculture was only empowered to expropriate the "estate or interest in or easement over land" that was "reasonably required" for the purposes of the canal, not more.
holdings.statement: The Minister of Agriculture applied for the lands at issue under section 21 of the Water Act, which allows expropriation of any land reasonably required for canal purposes, but no more.

holdings.quote: The Province could not do an end run around the limitations on its powers inherent in the Water Act
holdings.statement: The Province could not circumvent the limitations on its powers inherent in the Water Act by taking more land than reasonably required for the canal.

holdings.quote: This reasoning was sufficient to dispose of the appeal in Osoyoos. Having found that it had not been shown that anything more than a leasehold interest or an easement was "reasonably required" to construct, operate or maintain the canal within the meaning of the Water Act, the Court was bound to conclude that the Order in Council did not convey a greater interest (Osoyoos, paragraph 69).
holdings.statement: In Osoyoos, the Court found that only a leasehold interest or easement was reasonably required for the canal, so the Order in Council did not convey a greater interest.

holdings.quote: Irrespective of anything else, the provincial government could not take more, and the federal government could not grant more, than what the Water Act authorized.
holdings.statement: The provincial government could not take more, and the federal government could not grant more, than what the Water Act authorized.

holdings.quote: No such restriction exists here. On the contrary, the Highway Act as it read at the relevant time, contemplated that "Unless otherwise provided for, the soil and freehold of every public road shall be vested in His Majesty ..." (section 5). That this Act generally provides for the taking of a freehold in land rather than some lesser interest is not surprising.
holdings.statement: No such restriction exists in this case because the Highway Act contemplates that the soil and freehold of every public road shall be vested in His Majesty, generally providing for the taking of a freehold in land rather than a lesser interest.

holdings.quote: While every road can conceivably be built and operated on leased lands, or on a mere right of way, it would have made no sense in 1956, anymore than it would today, to build a major Highway on land held by a third party. The Appeal Judge's finding to that effect (reasons, paragraphs 23, 24 and 30) is based on the words of the Highway Act and plain common sense.
holdings.statement: It would have made no sense in 1956, or today, to build a major highway on land held by a third party, supporting the Appeal Judge's finding based on the Highway Act and common sense.

holdings.quote: The new evidence allowed in by my colleagues does not detract from the conclusion reached by the Appeal Judge on this point. It shows that exceptionally the Province took a lesser interest from Canadian Pacific Railway Company with respect to a limited strip within the 100 foot corridor running through part of the reserve.
holdings.statement: The new evidence showing the Province took a lesser interest from Canadian Pacific Railway Company for a limited strip within the corridor does not detract from the Appeal Judge's conclusion.

holdings.quote: The Highway Act expressly contemplates that the Province could take a lesser interest where "otherwise provided" (section 5).
holdings.statement: The Highway Act expressly contemplates that the Province could take a lesser interest where otherwise provided.

holdings.quote: I do not believe that the Appeal Judge in reaching the above noted conclusion proceeded on the basis that the provincial legislation was prima facie determinative of the terms of the transfer (Linden J.A., paragraph 58); his reasons make it clear that the only relevant intention is that of the Crown acting in its federal capacity.
holdings.statement: The Appeal Judge did not proceed on the basis that provincial legislation was determinative of the terms of the transfer; the relevant intention is that of the Crown acting in its federal capacity.

holdings.quote: However, in determining this intention, he found it useful to consider the request to which the grantor was responding (reasons, paragraphs 16, 17 and 18).
holdings.statement: In determining the Crown's intention, the Appeal Judge found it useful to consider the request to which the grantor was responding.

holdings.quote: I can detect no error in the approach adopted by the Appeal Judge. Indeed, the majority in Osoyoos specifically refers to paragraphs 13 to 19 of the reasons of the Appeal Judge in the present matter as reflecting the proper approach in matters such as this (Osoyoos, paragraph 47). The Appeal Judge nowhere departs from this framework of analysis.
holdings.statement: There is no error in the Appeal Judge's approach, which is consistent with the proper framework of analysis referred to by the majority in Osoyoos.

holdings.quote: In the end, only a clear and plain intention on the part of the federal government can support a conclusion that land has been removed from a reserve (reasons, paragraph 19).
holdings.statement: Only a clear and plain intention on the part of the federal government can support a conclusion that land has been removed from a reserve.

holdings.quote: The other crucial difference between the two Orders in Council lies in the last clause which deals with mineral rights.
holdings.statement: The other crucial difference between the two Orders in Council lies in the last clause dealing with mineral rights.

holdings.quote: In Osoyoos, the majority of the Judges, relying on a finding made by Lambert J.A. of the B.C. Court of Appeal, held that the reservation of mineral rights in that case was a "boiler plate" provision and thus not properly indicative of the intention of the grantor (Osoyoos, paragraph 79).
holdings.statement: In Osoyoos, the majority held that the reservation of mineral rights was a 'boiler plate' provision and thus not properly indicative of the grantor's intention.

holdings.quote: A "boiler plate" provision as these words suggest is a standard clause which is systematically reproduced usually verbatim in a series of instruments having the same object (Black's Law Dictionary, sixth edition, page 175). The fact that such clauses are automatically inserted appears to have led the majority in Osoyoos, to hold that, although the reservation of mineral rights was otherwise "quite instructive", no reliance could be placed on it.
holdings.statement: A 'boiler plate' provision is a standard clause systematically reproduced verbatim in a series of instruments having the same object, which led the majority in Osoyoos to hold no reliance could be placed on it despite its instructiveness.

holdings.quote: Accepting as I must, that the clause in Osoyoos was "boiler plate", as this term is usually understood, this last clause cannot possibly be labelled the same way.
holdings.statement: The clause in the Order in Council under review cannot be labelled as 'boiler plate' unlike the clause in Osoyoos.

holdings.quote: The comparison of the two orders makes it clear that in the present case, the federal government, in an obvious attempt to reconcile the public interest in having the subject lands used for Highway purposes and its fiduciary duty (as it then understood it) to minimally impair Indian interests in reserve land, carefully carved out of the interest granted to the Province, the ownership of mines and minerals, and provided for the right to "enter upon, use and occupy the said lands ... to such extent as may be necessary for ..." the exploitation of these mines and minerals (compare Osoyoos, paragraphs 52 to 55).
holdings.statement: The federal government carefully carved out ownership of mines and minerals from the interest granted to the Province and provided for the right to enter upon and use the lands to exploit these minerals.

holdings.quote: The principle of minimal impairment will tilt the balance in favour of the Indian interests wherever there is a "genuine" ambiguity in the intention of the federal government as evidenced by the instrument of conveyance (Osoyoos, paragraph 68).
holdings.statement: The principle of minimal impairment favors Indian interests where there is a genuine ambiguity in the federal government's intention as evidenced by the instrument of conveyance.

holdings.quote: A genuine ambiguity requires that there be a real doubt about the nature and extent of the interest conveyed.
holdings.statement: A genuine ambiguity requires a real doubt about the nature and extent of the interest conveyed.

holdings.quote: In the absence of any such doubt, it is incumbent upon the Courts to give effect to the clear and plain intention of the federal government.
holdings.statement: In the absence of genuine ambiguity, courts must give effect to the clear and plain intention of the federal government.

holdings.quote: In my view, it has not been shown when regard is had to the reasons of the Supreme Court in Osoyoos that a genuine ambiguity exists in this case or that the Appeal Judge erred in concluding that it was plain and obvious that the federal government by its Order in Council transferred to the Province absolute ownership of the subject lands save and except for the mines and minerals found to exist within, upon or under these lands.
holdings.statement: There is no genuine ambiguity in this case; the federal government transferred absolute ownership of the lands to the Province except for mines and minerals.

holdings.quote: In my view, the Appeal Judge, for the reasons that he gave, correctly concluded that the phrase "for road purposes" in the recital to the Order in Council did not render the fee determinable (reasons, paragraph 38).
holdings.statement: The Appeal Judge correctly concluded that the phrase 'for road purposes' did not render the fee determinable.

holdings.quote: Nor has it been shown that the Appeal Judge committed any error in holding that the corridor of land comprising the Lougheed Highway continues to be used for "road purposes" (reasons, paragraphs 36 and 37).
holdings.statement: The corridor of land comprising the Lougheed Highway continues to be used for 'road purposes'.

holdings.quote: I would dismiss the appeal with costs.
holdings.statement: The appeal is dismissed with costs.

authorities.quote: In correcting the same error made by the majority of the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Osoyoos Indian Band v. Oliver (Town), 1999 BCCA 297 (B.C.C.A.), the Supreme Court of Canada commented that "this approach is contrary to the clear and plain intention test for extinguishment" (Osoyoos, supra at para. 84). Rather, as explained in Osoyoos, supra at para. 69 (emphasis added), "the scope of the statutory power to transfer interests in land is constrained by the terms of the [provincial legislation]". The Governor in Council cannot grant more than the province is empowered to take, but can grant less (Osoyoos, supra at paras. 62, 69 ,136).
authorities.authority: The Supreme Court in Osoyoos held that the clear and plain intention test applies for extinguishment and that the scope of provincial statutory power constrains the transfer of interests in land.

authorities.quote: As Iacobucci J. explained (ibid. at para. 80):the only intention relevant to the inquiry is that of the grantor of the interest.
authorities.authority: Iacobucci J. explained that the only intention relevant is that of the grantor of the interest, here the Governor in Council.

authorities.quote: Gonthier J. also mentioned that "[i]t is for the government to decide, governed by its fiduciary obligation, the appropriate limits to the amount of land and the nature of the interest in land that it is transferring" (Osoyoos, supra at para. 134).
authorities.authority: Gonthier J. stated that the government decides the appropriate limits to the amount and nature of land interest transferred, governed by its fiduciary obligation.

authorities.quote: The Supreme Court was clear that the Crown's fiduciary obligation under s. 35 mandates that the Governor in Council "grant only the minimum interest required to fulfill [the] public purpose"(Osoyoos, supra at para. 52-55).
authorities.authority: The Supreme Court held that the Crown's fiduciary obligation under s. 35 mandates granting only the minimum interest required to fulfill the public purpose.

authorities.quote: As Iacobucci J. noted "as a general matter the Court should be reluctant to take away interests in land in the absence of conclusive evidence" (Osoyoos, supra at para. 65).
authorities.authority: Iacobucci J. noted courts should be reluctant to take away interests in land without conclusive evidence.

authorities.quote: The Supreme Court of Canada has found that less than absolute title can certainly suffice for the purposes of operating and maintaining a canal and, more importantly, building and maintaining a railway (see Canadian Pacific Ltd. v. Paul, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 654 at 671; and Osoyoos, supra).
authorities.authority: The Supreme Court found less than absolute title suffices for operating and maintaining canals and railways, and by analogy for highways absent contrary evidence.

authorities.quote: Although I am not sure whether the specific language of the prior grant was in evidence before the Supreme Court, the following comments of Iacobucci J. are apt in the circumstances. He explained, at para. 82 of Osoyoos, supra, that the prior grant of an easement "does not, by comparison, necessarily render the other two rights of way something other than an easement." These remarks were made in the context of analysing, by comparison, the internal language of the Osoyoos Order. His comments are even more applicable when comparing the language of two separate and distinct documents.
authorities.authority: The comments of Iacobucci J. in Osoyoos about prior grants of easements are apt and applicable when comparing language of separate documents.
